text: Dengue is a viral infection transmitted mainly by infected Aedes mosquitoes. It is common in tropical and subtropical areas.
Common dengue symptoms include high fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea and skin rash.
Dengue is caused by dengue viruses and is transmitted to people mainly through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.
Warning signs of severe dengue can include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, rapid breathing, weakness or restlessness. Serious warning signs require urgent medical evaluation.
Dengue prevention focuses on avoiding mosquito bites and reducing mosquito breeding sites around homes and communities.
Malaria is a potentially life-threatening disease caused by parasites transmitted through bites of infected mosquitoes.
Malaria commonly causes fever, chills and headache. Other symptoms can include sweating, weakness, nausea and body aches.
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites and is transmitted mainly through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
Severe malaria can become life-threatening and requires urgent medical assessment, particularly when a person becomes severely weak, confused or develops serious breathing or neurological problems.
Malaria prevention includes reducing exposure to mosquitoes and using appropriate mosquito-control measures in areas where malaria occurs.
Diabetes is a chronic condition in which blood glucose levels are elevated because the body does not produce enough insulin, does not use insulin effectively, or both.
Common symptoms of diabetes can include increased thirst, frequent urination, increased hunger, tiredness, blurred vision and unexplained weight changes.

Different forms of diabetes have different causes. Type 1 diabetes involves an autoimmune process that affects insulin production, while type 2 diabetes involves problems with insulin use and production.
Diabetes management can involve healthy eating, regular physical activity, monitoring blood glucose when advised, and following an individualized treatment plan from a healthcare professional.

Persistent symptoms such as excessive thirst, frequent urination, unexplained changes in weight or ongoing fatigue should be discussed with a healthcare professional and may require blood glucose testing.
Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition involving inflammation and narrowing of the airways that can cause breathing symptoms.
Asthma symptoms can include coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath and chest tightness. Symptoms can vary over time and may have different triggers.
Asthma symptoms may be triggered by allergens, tobacco smoke, air pollution, respiratory infections, exercise, cold air and other environmental factors.
Asthma care commonly involves identifying and reducing triggers, monitoring symptoms and following the asthma management plan provided by a healthcare professional.
Severe difficulty breathing or rapidly worsening breathing symptoms require urgent medical attention.
Influenza is a respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses and can affect people of all ages.
Influenza can cause sudden fever, cough, sore throat, muscle aches, headache, chills and fatigue.
Influenza is caused by influenza viruses and spreads mainly through respiratory droplets and particles from infected people.
Influenza prevention includes appropriate vaccination, hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene and avoiding close contact with people who are sick when possible.
Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria. It most commonly affects the lungs but can affect other parts of the body.
Pulmonary tuberculosis can cause prolonged cough, chest pain, weakness, fatigue, weight loss, fever and night sweats.
Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria and commonly spreads through the air when people with infectious pulmonary disease cough or sneeze.
A persistent cough, unexplained weight loss, prolonged fever or night sweats should be medically evaluated, particularly when tuberculosis exposure or risk is possible.
Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs that can be caused by bacteria, viruses or other microorganisms.
Pneumonia can cause cough, difficulty breathing, fever, chills and chest discomfort. Symptoms vary with the cause and the person.
Pneumonia may be caused by bacteria, viruses or other infectious organisms. The specific cause can vary between people.
Significant difficulty breathing, confusion, severe weakness or rapidly worsening symptoms require urgent medical evaluation.
Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is a condition in which the pressure of blood against artery walls is persistently elevated.
Many people with hypertension have no noticeable symptoms. Very high blood pressure can sometimes be associated with headache, blurred vision or other serious symptoms.
Risk factors for high blood pressure can include unhealthy diet, high salt intake, physical inactivity, tobacco use, harmful alcohol use and other health or genetic factors.
Healthy eating, reducing excessive salt intake, regular physical activity, avoiding tobacco and following professional medical advice can support blood pressure control.
Viral hepatitis is inflammation of the liver caused by hepatitis viruses. Different hepatitis viruses have different routes of transmission and health effects.
Viral hepatitis may cause tiredness, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, pale stools and yellowing of the skin or eyes. Some infections may cause few or no symptoms.
Viral hepatitis is caused by hepatitis viruses. Hepatitis A, B, C, D and E have different patterns of transmission and health effects.
Persistent symptoms suggestive of liver disease, including yellowing of the skin or eyes, unexplained fatigue or abdominal symptoms, should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.
Diarrhoeal disease involves frequent passage of loose or watery stools. It can be caused by infections, contaminated food or water and other factors.
Diarrhoeal illness commonly involves loose or watery stools and may also cause abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting or fever depending on the cause.
Replacing lost fluids is important during diarrhoeal illness. Oral rehydration solutions can help prevent dehydration when appropriate.
Safe drinking water, sanitation, handwashing and food hygiene are important measures for reducing diarrhoeal disease.
Signs of significant dehydration, blood in stool, severe weakness or persistent symptoms require medical evaluation.
Anaemia is a condition in which the number of red blood cells or their capacity to carry oxygen is lower than needed. Iron deficiency is a common cause.
Anaemia can be associated with tiredness, weakness, dizziness, shortness of breath and reduced ability to perform physical activities.
Anaemia can have several causes, including nutritional deficiencies, blood loss, infections, chronic diseases and inherited conditions.
Persistent tiredness, weakness, dizziness or shortness of breath should be discussed with a healthcare professional because different causes of anaemia require different evaluation.
Eczema is a group of inflammatory skin conditions that can cause dry, itchy and inflamed skin.

text: Eczema may cause dry skin, itching, redness, irritation and inflamed areas of skin. Symptoms can vary over time.
source: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: Skin care for eczema commonly includes regular moisturizing, avoiding known irritants and following a healthcare professional's treatment plan when symptoms are significant.
source: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: Acne is a common skin condition involving hair follicles and oil glands. It can cause pimples, blackheads, whiteheads and other skin lesions.
Acne can appear as blackheads, whiteheads, pimples and deeper inflammatory lesions, commonly affecting areas such as the face, chest and back.
Acne is associated with blocked hair follicles, oil production, skin-cell changes and inflammation. Hormonal changes can influence acne.
Severe, persistent or scarring acne may benefit from assessment by a healthcare professional or dermatologist.
Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluids than it takes in. It can occur with illness, vomiting, diarrhoea, sweating or inadequate fluid intake.
Dehydration can cause thirst, dry mouth, reduced urination, dark urine, tiredness, dizziness and weakness.
Dehydration can result from vomiting, diarrhoea, sweating, fever, inadequate fluid intake or conditions that increase fluid loss.
Severe dehydration can be serious. Markedly reduced urination, severe weakness, confusion or inability to keep fluids down require prompt medical attention.
The common cold is a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract. It commonly causes a runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing and sore throat.
Common cold symptoms can include runny nose, blocked nose, sneezing, sore throat, cough and mild tiredness.
The common cold is caused by viruses and can spread through respiratory droplets, contaminated surfaces and close contact with infected people.
Rest, adequate fluids and general supportive care can help with common cold symptoms. Persistent or severe symptoms may require medical assessment.
Headache is pain in the head or upper neck. Many different conditions can cause headaches, and the pattern and accompanying symptoms matter when evaluating the cause.
Headaches can have many causes, including tension, migraine, illness, dehydration, sleep problems, stress and other medical conditions.
A sudden, extremely severe headache or a headache accompanied by serious neurological symptoms should receive urgent medical evaluation.
Fever is a temporary increase in body temperature that can occur as part of the body's response to illness or infection.
Fever can occur with infections and other illnesses. The underlying cause depends on the person's symptoms and overall situation.
Fever may occur with chills, sweating, headache, weakness, muscle aches or other symptoms depending on its cause.
Persistent, very high or unexplained fever, especially when accompanied by serious symptoms, should be assessed by a healthcare professional.
Food poisoning can result from eating food or drinking water contaminated with harmful bacteria, viruses, parasites or toxins. Symptoms often involve the digestive system.
Foodborne illness may cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain or cramps and fever. Severity varies by cause and person.
Food poisoning can be caused by harmful bacteria, viruses, parasites or toxins in contaminated food or water.
Maintaining adequate fluid intake is important when vomiting or diarrhoea causes fluid loss. Persistent or severe illness requires medical assessment.
Severe dehydration, blood in stool or vomit, severe abdominal symptoms, confusion or persistent inability to keep fluids down require medical attention.
Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium and supports healthy bones. Low vitamin D levels can affect bone health.
Low vitamin D may affect bone health. Symptoms can be absent or nonspecific, so laboratory testing may be needed when deficiency is suspected.
Vitamin D status can be supported through appropriate dietary sources, safe sunlight exposure and supplements when recommended by a healthcare professional.
Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Iron deficiency can lead to iron-deficiency anaemia.
Iron deficiency can be associated with tiredness, weakness and other symptoms related to anaemia. Testing may be needed to confirm deficiency.
Iron can be obtained from foods including meat, beans, lentils and fortified foods. Iron supplements should be used with appropriate professional guidance when deficiency is suspected.
An allergy is an immune system reaction to a substance that is usually harmless to most people. Reactions can affect the skin, nose, eyes, lungs or digestive system.
Allergic reactions can cause sneezing, runny nose, itchy or watery eyes, skin symptoms or breathing symptoms depending on the allergen and person.
Common allergens can include pollen, dust mites, animal dander, certain foods, insect venom and some medicines or other substances.
Difficulty breathing, swelling of the throat or tongue, faintness or other signs of a severe allergic reaction require emergency medical attention.
Allergic rhinitis is an allergic reaction affecting the nose and can occur after exposure to allergens.
Allergic rhinitis can cause sneezing, itchy or watery eyes, runny nose and nasal congestion after exposure to an allergen.
Allergic rhinitis can be triggered by substances such as pollen, dust mites, mold and animal dander.
Constipation means having fewer bowel movements than usual or passing hard, dry stools that are difficult to pass.
Constipation can be associated with inadequate dietary fibre, insufficient fluid intake, low physical activity, changes in routine, certain medicines and some medical conditions.
Adequate fluids, appropriate dietary fibre and regular physical activity can support healthy bowel function when medically appropriate.
Persistent constipation, severe abdominal pain, vomiting or blood in the stool should be medically evaluated.
Migraine is a neurological condition that can cause recurrent headache attacks and may be accompanied by nausea or sensitivity to light and sound.
Migraine attacks can involve moderate to severe headache, nausea and sensitivity to light or sound. Some people experience warning symptoms called aura.
Migraine attacks may be associated with triggers such as changes in sleep, stress, certain foods, hormonal changes or environmental factors, although triggers differ between people.
Frequent, changing or unusually severe headaches should be discussed with a healthcare professional. Sudden severe headache or serious neurological symptoms require urgent evaluation.
Kidney stones are hard deposits that form in the kidneys. They can cause pain when they move through the urinary tract.
Kidney stones can cause severe pain in the side or back, pain that moves toward the lower abdomen or groin, painful urination, nausea or blood in the urine.
Kidney stones form when certain substances in urine become concentrated and form crystals. Different types of stones have different contributing factors.
Severe pain, fever with urinary symptoms, persistent vomiting or difficulty passing urine can require urgent medical evaluation.
A urinary tract infection is an infection affecting parts of the urinary system, including the bladder or urethra.
A urinary tract infection can cause symptoms such as pain or burning during urination, frequent urination and lower abdominal discomfort.
Urinary tract infections are commonly caused by bacteria entering and multiplying in the urinary tract.
Fever, chills, back or side pain, vomiting or worsening urinary symptoms can indicate a more serious infection and require medical assessment.
High environmental temperatures can cause heat-related health problems, particularly when the body cannot cool itself effectively.
Heat-related illness can involve heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea or other symptoms associated with overheating and fluid loss.
During high heat, people can reduce risk by staying hydrated, keeping cool, limiting strenuous activity during the hottest periods and checking on people who may be more vulnerable.
Severe heat-related illness can be dangerous. Confusion, loss of consciousness or rapidly worsening symptoms require urgent medical attention.
Good sleep supports physical and mental health. Sleep needs vary by age, and regular sleep routines can support healthy sleep.
Healthy sleep habits can include maintaining a regular sleep schedule, creating a comfortable sleep environment and developing a consistent bedtime routine.
Persistent sleep problems or excessive daytime sleepiness that interfere with daily activities should be discussed with a healthcare professional.
Self-care can include activities and choices that support health, prevent illness and help people manage aspects of their health with appropriate professional support when needed.
General health-supporting habits can include adequate sleep, balanced nutrition, physical activity appropriate for the individual, hydration, hygiene and seeking professional care when needed.
Self-care does not replace professional medical assessment. Persistent, severe or unexplained symptoms should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.
